newsitem.title: JAPAN: ASIAN METALS--Chile strikes seen supporting copper.
newsitem.headline: ASIAN METALS--Chile strikes seen supporting copper.

text.p: Ongoing strikes at Chilean copper mines are expected to support world copper prices in the short term, even though the strikes have not caused delivery delays to Japan so far, Japanese metal traders said on Thursday.
They also said physical trade in base metals would remain quiet this week in Japan due to the "Golden Week" holidays.
Chile, a major copper producer, has been hit by strikes at two of its copper mines, the giant Escondida mine and Quebrada Blanca.
A small group of workers at 800,000-tonne-a-year Escondida copper, owned by Broken Hill Proprietary and RTZ-CRA, has been on strike for a week and a half.
Workers at the 75,000-tonne-a-year Quebrada Blanca mine also went on strike on Wednesday after wage negotiations broke down.
Japanese smelters are major purchasers of copper concentrates from the Escondida mine, base metal industry officials said.

"We're certainly concerned about shipment delays. But the strikes have not caused actual shipment delays so far, probably because of ample stockpiles at Chilean ports," a copper trader with a major trading house said.
On the London Metal Exchange (LME), benchmark three-month copper on Wednesday ended at $2,379 a tonne, up $19 from the previous close.
Traders here said they expect LME copper to remain volatile, fluctuating between about $2,350 and $2,450 a tonne until late next week.
In the zinc market, China is still actively offering metal to regional buyers, due to the current strength in global zinc prices, Japanese traders said.
Three-month zinc on the LME ended at $1,273 per tonne on Wednesday, up nine dollars from the previous close.
"After LME zinc prices rose above the $1,200 level, Chinese traders boosted their offers," a zinc trader said.
He added that premiums for Special High Grade (SHG) zinc have edged up by nearly five dollars from last week's levels, because sellers other than China expect supply tightness to prevail for a while.
The physical aluminium market was quiet.

Japanese aluminium buyers are soon due to start negotiations with producers over premiums for third-quarter deliveries under long-term contracts, traders said. The premiums are likely to be lower in the July to September quarter than in the previous quarter, as an increase in Japan's sales tax on April 1 is expected to bite into economic growth, traders said.

About one-third of Japan's annual aluminium demand of some 2.4 million tonnes is sold under long-term contracts, while another third is from equity-related long-term deals and the remaining third from spot deals.
